## 1. Introduction
Previous research has identified inter-group contact and group membership
as an important factor in understanding prejudice [@allport1954; @pettigrew2006]. 
Research on minority influence suggests that committed minorities can
promote collective social change. Researchers Xie et al., 2011, used an opinion
dynamics model to further investigate how committed minorities can drive
social change [@xie2011social]. While researchers [@centola2018experimental] 
provided experimental evidence of tipping points in social convention change.  
Our proposed agent-based model adds prejudice towards a committed minority 
as a potential barrier to pro-immigration attitude adoption by the majority.
Research on source credibility researchers hypothesize that individuals will
be less receptive to agents if they belong to a different social group 
[@hovland1951credibility]. We will model prejudice as reducing receptiveness 
to influence from agents who are immigrants in the minority group. This is a
simplifying modelling assumption rather than a direct finding of the 
source-credibility research. We investigate how population size, committed 
minority proportion, and prejudice affect pro-immigration attitude adoption 
and the time required to achieve majority attitude reversal and or adoption. 
We also examine whether prejudice changes the committed minority proportion 
around which a sharp increase in successful adoption occurs (tipping point).

## 2. The model
title: "prejudice-tipping-abm: Prejudice and attitude-change tipping points"
The prejudice-tipping-abm examines how population size, committed minority
proportion, and prejudice discount affect the spread of pro-immigration 
attitudes.

##Agents and Inital Attitudes:

In the proposed initialization, immigrant minority agents hold a
pro-immigration attitude and remain committed to it throughout the simulation. 
All majority agents initially hold an anti-immigration attitude and are 
non-committed, allowing their attitudes to change. This initial division is a
simplifying modelling assumption, not a claim about the attitudes of real 
immigrant or majority populations.

Agents can hold an anti-immigration attitude, a pro-immigration attitude,
or both attitudes. The code uses NOT_PREJUDICED to identify the fully 
pro-immigration state and BOTH to identify the mixed state.

##Independent Variables: 
We vary three model parameters:
1. Population size (group_n): the total number of agents.
2. Minority proportion (minority_prop): the proportion of agents belonging 
to the committed immigrant minority.
3. Prejudice discount (prejudice_discount): a parameter between 0 and 1 that 
reduces receptiveness to minority speakers. When the speaker belongs to the 
minority, the hearer's update is permitted with probability 1 minus the 
prejudice discount. Higher values therefore mean stronger discounting of 
minority influence. When the speaker is not a minority agent, 
this discount does not block the hearer's update. Committed agents do 
not change their attitudes.

## Hearer Attitude Updates
During an interaction, hearer_updates 
indicates whether the hearer is permitted to update their attitude. 
TRUE (1) permits an update, provided the hearer is not committed; 
FALSE (0) blocks the hearer's update. It is a binary interaction-level 
indicator, not the prejudice parameter itself. If the hearer already holds 
the communicated attitude, either alone or as part of a mixed attitude, 
an allowed update leaves the hearer holding only the communicated attitude. 
Otherwise, an allowed update gives the hearer a mixed attitude. In the former 
case, a non-committed speaker also retains only the communicated attitude; 
the speaker's update is not gated by hearer_updates.

##Outcome measures
Adoption proportion is the proportion of non-committed agents who hold the 
fully pro-immigration attitude. Under the proposed initialisation, these are 
the initially anti-immigration majority agents. Committed minority agents are 
excluded from this measure. Mixed attitudes do not count as full adoption.
The adoption criterion is met when adoption proportion exceeds tip_level. 
If tip_level is set to 0.5, this means more than 50% of the non-committed 
agents hold a fully pro-immigration attitude. This is an operational success 
criterion, not a universal research threshold. Our planned primary outcomes are:
Final adoption proportion: adoption proportion at a common, 
fixed simulation endpoint, measured for every run.

Adoption proportion is calculated among majority agents only: the
number of initially anti-immigration majority agents who hold a fully
pro-immigration attitude, divided by the total number of majority
agents. Committed minority agents are excluded from both the numerator
and the denominator. This ensures that the measure reflects attitude
change in the majority and is not mechanically inflated by the
proportion of committed minority agents.

Adoption threshold reached: a binary indicator, coded 1 if the adoption
criterion is reached within the simulation period and 0 otherwise.
Our planned secondary outcome is rounds to adoption threshold: the first 
conversation round when the adoption criterion is reached. Runs that do not 
reach it are right-censored at the simulation time limit, meaning that the 
threshold-crossing time is not observed within that period.

##Current implementation and planned measurements

The current function returns the first threshold-crossing round and stops 
the run at that point. If the threshold is not reached within the simulation 
limit, it returns NA. Threshold attainment can therefore be derived from 
whether a crossing round is returned. To measure final adoption at a common 
endpoint, the implementation must record the first crossing round without 
ending the simulation early, continue to the fixed time limit, and return 
final adoption alongside the crossing time and success indicator. 
The simulation protocol must also specify what one conversation round
represents and the maximum number of rounds.

## Estimating a tipping threshold

For each combination of population size and prejudice discount, 
we plan to compare repeated simulations across minority proportions. 
We will assess whether final adoption or the probability of 
reaching the adoption criterion changes sharply around a particular minority
proportion. Reaching the adoption criterion within one run is not itself 
evidence of a tipping point. A tipping threshold is assessed from patterns
across parameter conditions and repeated runs. If outcomes change gradually, 
we will report that no clear tipping threshold was identified under the 
conditions tested.

## 3. Load the code
The model code lives in `src/`. These chunks are switched off until the files exist.

```{r load-code, eval=FALSE}
source("src/model.R")
source("src/analysis.R")
```

## 4. Example run
```{r example-run, eval=FALSE}
p   <- default_params()
res <- run_model(p, committed_share = 0.3, max_ticks = 100, record = TRUE)
head(res$history)
```
